extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journalists, fact‑checkers, and members of the public interested in disinformation and influence operations
extracted.subtask_description: Cataloging and identifying characteristics and behaviors of fake news websites and influence‑operation networks (domains, tactics, and infrastructure signals) used to mislead or manipulate audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoofing established publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Websites present themselves as or 'Spoof of' well‑known news outlets (e.g., 'Spoof of The Japan Times', 'Spoof of The Atlantic').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly across the list as a tactic to lend apparent credibility to false stories; many entries explicitly note which recognized outlet is being imitated.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDN homograph attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of internationalized domain names that replace characters to look like legitimate domains (the page cites 'IDN homograph attack' replacing 'i' with Turkish 'ı').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: xn--theguardan‑... that visually mimics 'theguardian' by substituting lookalike characters to fool readers and automated checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typosquatting / typo domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Domains intentionally misspelled to mimic legitimate sites (noted as 'Typosquatting' or examples like 'indepnedent.co').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typosquatting is listed as a recurring identifier of impostor sites that rely on user mistyping or quick glances to deceive readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masquerading as local outlets, NGOs, or national outlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites 'masquerade' as being based in particular countries or as NGOs/organizations to appear locally authoritative (e.g., 'Masquerades as a United Kingdom‑based news outlet', 'Masquerades as a Latin America‑based NGO').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tactic targets geographic or civic credibility to influence specific national/regional audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying or republishing content (plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites 'Copied from Wikipedia', 'copied content from other news websites', or are described as republishing/rephrasing stories from established outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent sign of low‑effort disinformation or content farms; examples include Mission and content farm networks that repeatedly republish material from legitimate sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content farm behavior / sensational false content
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks described as 'content farm' that post sensational and false articles (e.g., Happytify by Wuwei Technologies described as a content farm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by mass production of low‑quality, sensational pieces designed for attention rather than factual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link wheeling to manipulate search engine rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of 'link wheeling' strategies to influence Google/Bing rankings (explicitly mentioned as a technique).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sites and networks engage in SEO manipulation to increase visibility and apparent legitimacy in search results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared ad/analytics identifiers (infrastructure linking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sites share Google AdSense and Google Analytics IDs, indicating common operators or coordinated infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared IDs are a forensic signal linking ostensibly separate sites to the same operator(s); noted in Philippine examples where many sites shared IDs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated quotes and false claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites publishing invented quotations or fabricated assertions (example: fabricated quotes from John Scarlett, false claims about Macron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabricated sourcing or invented quotes are highlighted as direct evidence of deliberate disinformation rather than mere bias or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ephemeral disinformation (delete-after-engagement tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactic where an article is deleted after gaining engagement and URLs are redirected to the website the article was falsely portraying — labeled 'ephemeral disinformation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizen Lab described Endless Mayfly as using this technique: remove content after it spreads to erase traces and avoid prolonged scrutiny while still amplifying the falsehood briefly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of generative AI to produce content
rubrics_metrics.description: Networks used generative AI models (e.g., ChatGPT) to generate articles and social media comments; OpenAI and Microsoft analyses noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Storm‑2035 and other networks where content or comments were authored by AI, sometimes reposting U.S. outlet content without attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake social media accounts, bot networks, and hijacked accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of inauthentic social media accounts, bot promotion networks, and hijacked accounts to amplify sites (multiple mentions of accounts taken down for 'coordinated inauthentic behavior').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform enforcement actions (Facebook/Twitter takedowns) are repeatedly cited; these networks often include bots or compromised accounts used to amplify content.

rubrics_metrics.name: GAN‑generated profile pictures and synthetic identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Social profiles used by campaigns sometimes used profile pictures created by generative adversarial networks (GANs) and possibly hijacked accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Zeno Zeno campaign employed GAN‑generated images for profiles, a sign of synthetic network assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated inauthentic behavior (platform enforcement signal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated platform takedowns for 'coordinated inauthentic behavior' are cited as evidence of organized influence operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several networks and their associated social media assets were removed by Meta/Twitter/Google for coordinated inauthentic behavior; the label is used as an operational descriptor and enforcement outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private marketing / PR firms acting for state or political actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Private firms were implicated in running influence operations on behalf of governments or political clients (e.g., Shenzhen Haimaiyunxiang, UReputation, Stoic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizen Lab, Microsoft, and other reports emphasize the role of third‑party firms in designing and executing digital influence campaigns, demonstrating state or political outsourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted audience segmentation (geographic/demographic targeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns deliberately target specific audiences (examples: Black Americans, the Chinese diaspora, young left‑leaning residents in the U.S. and Canada).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listings frequently note the intended audience or country focus, indicating purposeful segmentation to maximize influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backdating content and false copyright (DMCA) takedown abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics include backdating blog posts and filing DMCA takedowns to suppress original content, as alleged in the Tanzanian case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are manipulative techniques to manufacture apparent prior publication or to remove competing content through false copyright claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of advertising revenue and Google publishing partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Some networks place ads via Google (and are described as Google publishing partners) to monetize and distribute content that mixes disinformation with ads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ProPublica found ad placements on sites described as mixing anti‑immigrant and vaccine disinformation with advertising; ad partnerships can both fund and legitimize such sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure or legal enforcement actions as indicators of illicit networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Several domains have been 'Seized by the United States federal government' or otherwise acted against by authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seizure is cited as a status that confirms law‑enforcement attention and may be used as post‑hoc evidence of illicit or coordinated activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain switching and repeated renaming to evade bans
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators repeatedly switch domain names to evade platform or enforcement bans (explicitly noted for Mission and other networks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent domain churn is an operational tactic to stay ahead of blocks and to continue distribution after takedowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repackaging and rebroadcasting state media through ostensibly independent sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Clusters of sites 'aggressively repackaged and re‑broadcast Iranian state media' or other state outlets while presenting as independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IUVM and similar networks are described as rebroadcasting state content under a façade of independence — a mark of state‑linked influence operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious journalists / lack of digital footprint for bylined staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists listed on sites often have no identifiable digital footprint or have suspended accounts, suggesting fabricated or untraceable staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple entries note that bylined 'journalists' either have suspended accounts or cannot be independently verified, a sign of inauthentic staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fabricated endorsements or fictitious celebrity ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Some networks used ads with fictitious celebrity endorsements (e.g., AdStyle examples) to lend credibility or attract clicks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fake ads are used as part of engagement strategies and to monetize or promote trust through false social proof.
